# Positioning vs Messaging vs Branding: Which Is Broken?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/positioning-vs-messaging-vs-branding/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-07 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Positioning is the decision about where the company sits, messaging is the words that carry it, and branding is how the company is recognized. Diagnose and fix them in that order, because a brand refresh cannot fix a positioning problem. A five-person sentence test shows which layer is broken.

When marketing isn't connecting with buyers, a rebrand may be the wrong first fix. Positioning is the decision about what the company is, for whom and against what alternative. Messaging is the words that carry that decision. Branding is the system that makes the company recognizable and remembered between contacts. They are done in that order, and the cheapest test of which one is broken is to ask five people in the company to finish one sentence.

When a company says its marketing "isn't landing," the diagnosis is usually one of three problems wearing the same symptoms. Positioning, messaging, and branding are different jobs, done in a particular order, and fixing the wrong one is expensive.

|  | Positioning | Messaging | Branding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A decision about where the company sits | The words that carry the decision | The system that makes the company recognizable |
| Main output | Buyer, problem, alternative, category, reason to choose | Problem statement, promise, proof, objection answers | Name, mark, visual identity, tone, consistent behavior |
| Who owns it | The CEO or business owner, with a small team | Marketing, from customer evidence | Marketing and design |
| Broken when | People describe different customers | The site is accurate and still unclear | The company looks different on every surface |
| Typical fix | A workshop and a decision | A week of writing | A design project |

## Positioning: the decision about where you sit

Positioning is the choice of what the company is, for whom, and against what alternative. It is a decision, not a document. It answers: which buyer, which problem, which category the buyer will put us in, and why we are the better choice inside that category.

April Dunford's method breaks the decision into five components, worked in a set order: competitive alternatives (what customers would do if you did not exist), distinct capabilities, differentiated value, best-fit customers, and market category. She argues the category should come last, and that starting with it is "the tail wagging the dog." A category's job, in her words, is to take a prospect who knows little about the product and "point them in the direction of your differentiated value." A poor category forces sales and marketing to spend their time undoing wrong assumptions.

A fintech product can be positioned as a bank alternative, a savings tool, a treasury product for small businesses, or an embedded feature for other platforms. Each is a different buyer, a different competitor set, and a different price. The product may be identical. The company is not.

Positioning is broken when different people in the company describe a different customer, when prospects compare the product with things it was never meant to compete with, or when sales conversations begin with a long explanation of what category the product belongs to. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the alternative when the main rival is inaction and a dozen people decide.

## Messaging: the words that carry the position

Messaging is the set of things the company says to make the position land: the problem statement, the promise, the proof, the objections answered, the phrases used consistently across every surface. It depends entirely on positioning; messaging written before the position is decided is copy in search of a strategy.

Dunford makes the same dependency explicit: "Everything we do downstream from positioning - creating messaging, building a sales pitch deck, creating other marketing and sales materials - is all oriented around helping our best-fit customers understand our value."

Good messaging uses the buyer's language for the problem, states the change the product makes rather than the features that make it, and matches proof to the buyer's actual doubts.

Messaging is broken when the website describes the product accurately and prospects still do not understand what it is for, when sales uses different words from marketing, or when the most common objection in calls appears nowhere on the site. The second symptom is common. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them.

## Branding: how the company is recognized

Branding is the system of recognition: name, mark, visual identity, tone of voice, and the consistent behavior that makes the company feel like one thing across time. It is what remains in a buyer's memory between contacts.

That memory is most of the job in B2B, because most buyers are not buying. John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, in a 2021 report for LinkedIn's B2B Institute, estimated that about 20% of business buyers are in market over a year and roughly 5% in any quarter; he calls the "95-5 rule" a heuristic, not a law. Brands are chosen when a buyer enters the market and recalls them. The same report found well-established brands linked to only 20% to 30% of buyers' category entry points, with market leaders around 50%. Category entry points, a concept developed by Jenni Romaniuk at Ehrenberg-Bass, are the buying situations a brand should be linked to in memory. Our piece [Measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers how to track them.

Branding is broken when the company looks different on every surface, when the visual identity contradicts the position (a compliance-grade product that looks like a consumer game), or when nobody can describe the company's tone.

> Six months later the marketing still is not landing, now in a nicer font.

## The order

Positioning first, because everything else depends on the decision. Messaging second, because it carries the decision into words. Branding third, or in parallel with messaging, because the identity should express the position rather than precede it.

Companies routinely do this backward. They commission a brand refresh because the site "feels dated," write new copy to fit the new design, and never revisit the positioning that was the actual problem. Six months later the marketing still is not landing, now in a nicer font.

The order also explains why brand work is not wasted when it comes last. Memory structures take years to build, so a brand that encodes the wrong position is expensive to unwind. Building it on a settled position means the recognition it earns points at the right buyer and the right buying situations.

## A quick diagnostic

Ask five people in the company to write one sentence: we help [who] do [what] instead of [alternative]. If the sentences differ, the problem is positioning. If they agree and the website does not say it plainly, the problem is messaging. If the website says it plainly and the company is still forgettable or inconsistent, the problem is branding.

| Result of the five-sentence test | Broken layer | First fix | Relative cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The sentences name different buyers or alternatives | Positioning | A positioning workshop, ending in a written decision | Low: time from senior people |
| The sentences agree, the site does not say it | Messaging | Rewrite from customer calls and objection logs | Low: about a week of writing |
| The site says it, buyers still forget or confuse you | Branding | A design and identity project built on the position | Higher: external design spend |

Fix in that order. Positioning is a workshop and a decision. Messaging is a week of writing from customer evidence. Branding is a design project. Only the last one costs much money, and it is the one least likely to be the problem. If the problem turns out to be in a pitch deck rather than the website, [The story isn't landing](https://lowob.com/research/the-story-isnt-landing/) applies the same logic to investors.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the buyer and competitive alternative before polishing copy.** Positioning is the decision everything else carries.
- **Make the message explain the position clearly.** Use the buyer's words, state the change, match proof to doubts.
- **Let the visual identity reinforce a decision already made.** In B2B, brand mostly works through memory when buyers enter the market.
- **Diagnose before spending.** The five-sentence test costs an afternoon; a rebrand costs months.
